claims.statement: The Mauryan dynasty brought much of the Indian subcontinent under one ruling house. Chandragupta founded it, followed by Bindusara and Ashoka. Its capital was Pataliputra. The connections here follow the rulers, their dealings with Alexander’s successors and the surviving evidence of Ashoka’s reign.

value.text: The Mauryan dynasty brought much of the Indian subcontinent under one ruling house. Chandragupta founded it, followed by Bindusara and Ashoka. Its capital was Pataliputra. The connections here follow the rulers, their dealings with Alexander’s successors and the surviving evidence of Ashoka’s reign.

claims.statement: The Mauryan Empire: 321 BCE to 185 BCE. Approximate dynastic chronology follows the Met’s main text, 321–185 BCE; its heading uses 323. No fixed territorial border is implied.

value.text: The Mauryan Empire: 321 BCE to 185 BCE. Approximate dynastic chronology follows the Met’s main text, 321–185 BCE; its heading uses 323. No fixed territorial border is implied.

claims.statement: Chandragupta took power in Magadha and established the Mauryan dynasty. His expansion connected the Ganges valley with the north-west, where Alexander’s successors were competing for control. He reached a settlement with Seleucus. Bindusara succeeded him; the date of that succession is approximate.

claims.statement: Chandragupta Maurya’s reign: 321 BCE to 297 BCE. Reign, not lifespan. Uses Livius’s conventional 321–c.297 BCE chronology. Early Mauryan chronology is debated.

value.text: Chandragupta Maurya’s reign: 321 BCE to 297 BCE. Reign, not lifespan. Uses Livius’s conventional 321–c.297 BCE chronology. Early Mauryan chronology is debated.

claims.statement: Bindusara succeeded his father Chandragupta and was followed by his son Ashoka. His reign sits between two better documented rulers. Accounts attribute expansion in central India to him, but some assign the same conquests to Ashoka. The division is uncertain.

value.text: Bindusara succeeded his father Chandragupta and was followed by his son Ashoka. His reign sits between two better documented rulers. Accounts attribute expansion in central India to him, but some assign the same conquests to Ashoka. The division is uncertain.

claims.statement: Bindusara’s reign: 297 BCE to 272 BCE. Approximate reign, not lifespan, following Livius. Other chronologies place the succession to Ashoka differently.

value.text: Bindusara’s reign: 297 BCE to 272 BCE. Approximate reign, not lifespan, following Livius. Other chronologies place the succession to Ashoka differently.

claims.statement: Ashoka was the third Mauryan emperor. He supported Buddhism and had inscriptions placed across his empire. These surviving texts make his rule unusually visible. They let us compare what a king said about government and conduct with the monuments and places connected to his reign.

value.text: Ashoka was the third Mauryan emperor. He supported Buddhism and had inscriptions placed across his empire. These surviving texts make his rule unusually visible. They let us compare what a king said about government and conduct with the monuments and places connected to his reign.

claims.statement: Ashoka’s reign: 273 BCE to 232 BCE. Reign, not lifespan. The Met uses c.273–232 BCE; Livius gives accession in 272. Accession and coronation chronologies differ. No birth date is inferred.

value.text: Ashoka’s reign: 273 BCE to 232 BCE. Reign, not lifespan. The Met uses c.273–232 BCE; Livius gives accession in 272. Accession and coronation chronologies differ. No birth date is inferred.

claims.statement: Ashoka used inscriptions on rock and polished stone pillars to communicate beyond his court. They recorded royal instructions and ideas about conduct. The surviving inscriptions are evidence of particular statements in particular places, rather than proof that every subject lived by the same rules.

value.text: Ashoka used inscriptions on rock and polished stone pillars to communicate beyond his court. They recorded royal instructions and ideas about conduct. claims.statement: Ashoka’s rock and pillar inscriptions: 254 BCE to 232 BCE. Editorial window from the Met’s starting date of 254 BCE to the end of Ashoka’s reign. Not a continuous carving programme or the date of every edict.

value.text: Ashoka’s rock and pillar inscriptions: 254 BCE to 232 BCE. Editorial window from the Met’s starting date of 254 BCE to the end of Ashoka’s reign. Not a continuous carving programme or the date of every edict.

claims.statement: Seleucus served under Alexander and later established a kingdom of his own. He sought refuge with Ptolemy in Egypt before recovering power in Babylonia. His settlement with Chandragupta connects the struggles among Alexander’s successors with the rise of the Mauryan state. He was assassinated in 281 BCE.

value.text: Seleucus served under Alexander and later established a kingdom of his own. He sought refuge with Ptolemy in Egypt before recovering power in Babylonia. His settlement with Chandragupta connects the struggles among Alexander’s successors with the rise of the Mauryan state. He was assassinated in 281 BCE.

claims.statement: Seleucus I Nicator: 358 BCE to 281 BCE. Approximate birth c.358 BCE; death 281 BCE. Lifespan, not reign. No continuous personal itinerary is inferred.

value.text: Seleucus I Nicator: 358 BCE to 281 BCE. Approximate birth c.358 BCE; death 281 BCE. Lifespan, not reign. No continuous personal itinerary is inferred.

claims.statement: Chandragupta and Seleucus reached a settlement after conflict near the Indus. Their agreement connected the Mauryan state with one of the kingdoms formed after Alexander’s death. The early evidence does not clearly establish who won the fighting. Later accounts have turned that uncertainty into very different stories.

claims.statement: Chandragupta and Seleucus make peace: 305 BCE to 303 BCE. One episode within approximately 305–303 BCE, following Jansari’s publisher synopsis. This range does not establish three years of uninterrupted warfare or a precise treaty date.

claims.statement: Pataliputra was the Mauryan capital. The Greek envoy Megasthenes described a city defended by a timber wall, gates and towers. That account gives us a view of the capital through a visitor’s writing. It should not be treated as a complete description of everyday life there.

claims.statement: Pataliputra under the Mauryas: 321 BCE to 185 BCE. Editorial window follows the dynasty, not the foundation or end of the city. Megasthenes’ description is literary testimony. A precise map reference has not yet been checked.

claims.statement: Lumbini is a Buddhist pilgrimage site in what is now southern Nepal. Its archaeological remains include Ashoka’s inscribed pillar and structures dating back to the third century BCE. The pillar connects the place to a recorded royal visit, alongside the longer history of worship at the site.

value.text: Lumbini is a Buddhist pilgrimage site in what is now southern Nepal. Its archaeological remains include Ashoka’s inscribed pillar and structures dating back to the third century BCE. The pillar connects the place to a recorded royal visit, alongside the longer history of worship at the site.

claims.statement: Lumbini: 300 BCE to 201 BCE. Third-century BCE study window, not the lifespan of the site. UNESCO’s traditional date for the Buddha’s birth is not used here. The point is the World Heritage property reference.

value.text: Lumbini: 300 BCE to 201 BCE. Third-century BCE study window, not the lifespan of the site. UNESCO’s traditional date for the Buddha’s birth is not used here. The point is the World Heritage property reference.

claims.statement: Ashoka visited Lumbini and erected an inscribed pillar there. UNESCO dates the pillar to 249 BCE. This is a dated connection between a ruler and a place, rather than a general assumption that he visited every site associated with his dynasty.

claims.statement: Ashoka’s visit to Lumbini: 249 BCE to 249 BCE. Year follows UNESCO. The map uses the property reference, not a reconstructed route.

claims.statement: Taxila preserves several successive settlements. The Bhir mound contains the remains of an early historic town; Sirkap and Sirsukh belong to later phases. Its position brought it into contact with Persia, the Greek world and Central Asia. Buddhist monasteries and monuments were part of its changing urban landscape.

claims.statement: Taxila: 500 BCE to 200 CE. 500 BCE–200 CE is an editorial window within a much longer history. The point marks Bhir Mound, one component of the UNESCO property, not all Taxila or a political border.

claims.statement: Alexander entered Taxila in 326 BCE. UNESCO associates this episode with the Bhir mound, the earliest historic settlement in the archaeological complex. The city’s history extends beyond that encounter. Its other entries and connections put the campaign alongside the region’s urban and religious history.
